name: Google
summary: Google says it uses structured interviews: candidates for a role get similar questions, scored against shared rubrics, and its re:Work guide to structured interviewing describes assessing role-related knowledge, problem solving and leadership. Candidates commonly report coding interviews in a shared doc, system design for experienced roles, a 'Googleyness and leadership' interview, and a hiring committee that reviews the feedback before an offer.
rounds: One or two technical phone screens (coding in a shared doc)
Onsite or virtual loop: coding, system design (for experienced roles), and a 'Googleyness and leadership' interview
looks_for: General cognitive ability: how you reason through an open problem
Googleyness: comfort with ambiguity, collaboration, doing the right thing

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to work through a problem with no clear owner or direction.
covers: Why nobody owned it and what it would cost if nobody acted
How you created structure: defined the problem, found the right people, agreed next steps
What happened, and what you'd do the same or differently

questions.text: How would you estimate how many people use Google Maps on a weekday morning in Bengaluru?
covers: A clear structure: population, share with smartphones, share travelling in the morning, share who open Maps
Assumptions stated out loud with round numbers, and a sanity check at the end
Which assumption moves the answer most, and how you'd check it with data

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped a teammate who was struggling.
covers: How you noticed, and what was really getting in their way
What you did that helped without taking over their work
How they and the work were doing afterwards

questions.text: Walk me through the hardest technical decision you've made and the trade-offs you weighed.
covers: The options you had and the constraints: time, scale, team skills, cost
How you compared them: data, a prototype, or advice from others
What you chose, what it cost you, and whether it held up later

questions.text: Tell me about a time you changed your mind after getting new information.
covers: Your original view and why it was reasonable at the time
The data or argument that changed it
How you told others and what changed in the work

questions.text: Tell me about a time you led something without having any formal authority.
covers: The goal and why people didn't have to follow you
How you brought them along: listening, a clear plan, sharing credit
The outcome and what you learned about leading peers

questions.text: How would you design a service that suggests search queries as someone types?
covers: Requirements first: latency per keystroke, languages, freshness, personalisation
A prefix index ranked by popularity, with caching close to users
Filtering harmful suggestions, and how you'd measure whether suggestions help

questions.text: A web page loads slowly for some users but not for others. How would you find out why?
covers: Splitting by region, device, network and browser before guessing
Evidence from browser timings, server logs and tracing across services
Likely causes such as a slow dependency, a cache miss or heavy assets, and how you'd confirm one

questions.text: How would you remove duplicates from a list too large to fit in memory? Talk me through the trade-offs.
covers: The in-memory answer first, such as a hash set, and its time and space cost
Scaling out: sorting in chunks and merging, or hashing records into partitions
Approximate options like a Bloom filter when a small error rate is acceptable

questions.text: How would you improve Google Maps for people who travel mostly by bus or metro?
covers: One user group and its biggest pain points, such as waiting times or crowding
Two or three ideas, ranked by impact and effort
A success metric, plus a guardrail so other users aren't worse off

questions.text: How would you test whether a change to search results actually made them better for users?
covers: Defining 'better': one main metric plus guardrails such as speed
An experiment design: who is in it, how long it runs, how large it must be
Watching for novelty effects and differences between user groups

questions.text: Why Google, and which product or team would you most like to work on?
covers: A specific product or team and the problem it solves
Something you've built or studied that connects to it
What you hope to learn or contribute there

questions.text: Which Google product do you use most, and what would you change about it?
covers: A product you know well and one clear problem with it
The change, who it helps, and what you'd leave out
How you'd know it worked

questions.text: Where do you want your career to be in a few years, and how would this role help?
covers: A realistic direction: the skills or scope you want to grow into
How this role builds towards it
What you'd bring to the team along the way

tips: Think out loud: they score how you reason, not only the answer.
State assumptions, then test them; ask clarifying questions before you dive in.
For coding, talk through complexity and edge cases before you write.
Candidates commonly report coding in a plain shared doc: practise writing clean code without autocomplete or running it.
For the Googleyness and leadership interview, prepare stories about ambiguity, helping others and leading without a title.
Google says it scores structured interviews against rubrics, so answer the question you were asked fully before adding extras.

sources.title: Google re:Work: a guide to structured interviewing
